evals.prompt: Lay out the stream for our new onboarding assistant: three code changes (the welcome flow, the AI's first-session prompt, the progress checklist), each shipped in its own PR. Once all three are on staging we want to check how the AI actually behaves across them with about eight test sessions, and I want to see the session plan before any of them runs. Then I'll try it myself before we call it done.
evals.expected_behavior: Creates three top-level code tasks and one test task for the onboarding system that depends on all three; the code tasks never depend on it. The test task's What lists its cases, what each proves and a run budget of about eight sessions; its subtasks are its levels (the session plan to approve, then the runs), never one subtask per case, and no case is repeated in a code task's Done when. The user's own try is the reviewer's yes on the test task, not a separate acceptance task. Each Definition of Success clause has a task whose Done when delivers it.

evals.prompt: For the Q3 launch stream we ship a new pricing page and a new newsletter signup flow. Each one gets tested with five real customers after it is published. Set up the tasks.
evals.expected_behavior: Two deliverable tasks and two separate test tasks, one per system (pricing page, signup flow), since each customer test needs its own protocol and budget; each depends only on the deliverable it tests and holds its cases and its five-customer budget. Not one shared test task, not one task per customer or per case, and no umbrella task.

evals.prompt: Here are five unrelated bugs from support (date picker off by one, CSV export encoding, avatar upload limit, typo in the invite email, slow search on archived tasks). Each fix has its unit tests in its own PR. Put them on the board in the maintenance stream.
evals.expected_behavior: Five flat top-level tasks, no phases, no umbrella, and no test task for a check the PR's own tests cover; a test task appears only for a test judged needed, such as a post-merge test the user names, and a deploy task only for a deploy another member runs.

evals.prompt: Where does the Pad stream stand today? Just give me the short version.
evals.expected_behavior: Does not open the planning skill: a status question is answered from context.

evals.prompt: We should compare our two prompts properly. Set up a bench of runs on them so we know which one is better.
evals.expected_behavior: Opens the planning skill and, before the first run, writes the decision, the cheapest sufficient method, a numeric ceiling with its stop rule, and a failing and a sound case in the task, then shows them to the person.

evals.prompt: The diagnosis is clear: the AI skips the spec because the rule is only served at session start. I'll write a one-line reminder that the server sends at every message, and I can change its text on the server at any time. Before we build it, replay this morning's 300k-token conversation a few times with and without the line to check it works.
evals.expected_behavior: Opens the planning skill before proposing any run. Weighs what a wrong line would do before it is corrected (one sentence the server can change, whose failure leaves today's skipped reads in place) against the replay's cost, recommends building the line and checking real use, and proposes no replay. Any test it still offers comes with its decision and ceiling; it asks for no go on a protocol it has not shown.

evals.prompt: Run the unit tests for the date picker fix and tell me if they pass.
evals.expected_behavior: Runs the tests without opening the planning skill or writing a test protocol: a routine check that launches no AI session and takes no one's time or money is not a costly test.

evals.prompt: Tomorrow our outreach AI sends 5,000 emails to prospects, and sent emails can't be recalled. Last week it invented a customer name in a few drafts; we changed its prompt. Before the send, check it no longer does that.
evals.expected_behavior: The send cannot be undone, so it never recommends sending and watching. It protects the send either with a check of the drafts before they go, or with a small test whose decision on pass, fail and inconclusive, ceiling on runs and tokens, and stop rule it shows before asking the go. It runs nothing before that go.

evals.prompt: Plan the move of our invoicing to Stripe: export the customers, map the plans, switch the checkout, then turn the old system off. Probably two or three weeks.
evals.expected_behavior: It describes the work to the stream route and reads each returned stream's one-liner. When none covers invoicing or billing, it opens a new stream for this effort itself, with its rationale and definition of success, lays out the tasks in it, and says in its reply which stream and workspace it filed them in. It never asks the person which stream or workspace to use, and never asks whether to create the stream.

evals.prompt: Add the onboarding email fixes to the plan: the welcome email has a broken link and the reminder goes out twice. (The stream search returns two streams: "Signup flow", one-liner "Make account creation shorter and clearer"; and "Lifecycle emails", one-liner "The emails customers get after they sign up".)
evals.expected_behavior: It files both fixes in "Lifecycle emails", whose one-liner fits the work closest, and says so in one line. It asks no question about where to put them and opens no new stream.

evals.prompt: I'm not technical at all, I just want our customers to stop getting logged out every morning. Can you plan that?
evals.expected_behavior: Any question it asks frames the person's intent in their words: what result they expect, how they will know it works, what must not change. It asks no technical question (no session lifetime, token, cookie or framework question) and settles the technical choices from the sources or leaves them to the tasks. It files the work itself and says where.

evals.prompt: Set a goal for us: 50 active accounts by March 31, because the seed extension we need depends on it. We have 12 today. Leave enterprise deals out of it.
evals.expected_behavior: Creates the goal with its framing fields, not lines in `description`: `rationale` says why it matters now (the seed extension) and why March 31; `success_criterion` says how it is judged met; `nature` is "number" with `baseline_value` 12, `target_value` 50 and a unit such as active accounts; `deadline` is March 31; `goal_scope` leaves enterprise deals out. It invents no guardrail or stop condition the user did not give, and writes no "Why now:" or "Deadline" line in `description`.

evals.prompt: We decided as a team: the onboarding goal comes before the pricing goal this quarter, nothing technical forces it, it's where we get the most signal.
evals.expected_behavior: Writes that order and its reason (most signal first, a team choice) in the `description` of both goals concerned, after reading them. Adds no dependency between their streams or tasks, and does not put the order only in the user's Pad priorities.

evals.prompt: Create a stream for redoing the signup emails. (The workspace already has an active stream 'Onboarding emails', under another goal, whose one-liner covers the signup sequence.)
evals.expected_behavior: Before creating, reads the active streams nearest in meaning (`build_context(mode: "work_stream", query)`), then the links of 'Onboarding emails'. Proposes reusing 'Onboarding emails' for this work, or creating the new stream linked to it with a one-line reason; never creates an unlinked duplicate.

evals.prompt: Leave the 'Partner portal' stream as it is, I know it looks finished but I want to keep it open for the next partner.
evals.expected_behavior: Writes in the stream's update (`work_streams` `set_status`) that the user keeps it open on purpose and why (waiting for the next partner), so no AI proposes its cleanup again. Changes neither its status nor its tasks.

evals.prompt: For my own work this week I want to do the pricing page before the onboarding copy, no reason other than my energy.
evals.expected_behavior: Keeps that order in the user's priorities through the `octopad-pad` skill, section "Priorities", with its reason in the `why:` of the priority it concerns. Writes nothing in any goal's description and adds no dependency.

evals.prompt: Pause the 'Partner API' stream until the legal review is back. (Reading it shows its link to 'Billing v2' marked to review.)
evals.expected_behavior: After the pause, checks the stream once: reads each open top-level task in one line and the links marked to review. For 'Billing v2', checks that stream itself, not only the link: corrects it if the change alters what it assumes, then confirms the link as the read's line on links to review says, keeping every other link the stream holds. Changes no other stream's status.

evals.prompt: The review of 'Import CSV contacts' found two bugs. Open the fixes as tasks in the same stream, and add a task to write the import docs while you're at it.
evals.expected_behavior: Creates the three tasks with batch_tasks, then in the same turn adds a link of kind `link` from each fix task to 'Import CSV contacts' with tasks link_dependency, each line in the fix's voice saying what it takes from the review (for example the bug the review found), not a vague 'related to'. Gives the docs task no link to the reviewed task unless its line passes the test (it would need to know if that task changed or ended); uses depends_on only for a real wait.

evals.prompt: Link the 'Pricing page copy' stream to the 'Pricing page redesign' stream, they're both about pricing.
evals.expected_behavior: Checks the test before linking: a shared topic alone gets no link. Asks or checks whether one stream changes what the other assumes (for example the copy must fit the redesign's layout); if so, sends the links of the stream that depends on that fact with a link of kind `link` whose line names it in that stream's voice, at most 160 characters, keeping the links it already holds; if one truly waits on the other, uses `depends_on` instead. Never writes a line such as 'both about pricing'.

evals.prompt: Don't close the 'Partner portal' stream, keep it.
evals.expected_behavior: Writes in the stream's update (`work_streams` `set_status`) that the user keeps it open on purpose, with no invented reason since the user gave none. Changes neither its status nor its tasks.
